extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, filmmakers, scholars, and activists interested in racial representation in film/theatre/television
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge practices in film, theatre, television, and animation that affect portrayal of East and other Asian peoples—especially instances of yellowface, whitewashing, stereotyping, and casting. Useful for critics, programmers, and creators assessing authenticity and harms in media portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid yellowface / theatrical makeup caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellowface, a form of theatrical makeup used by European-American performers to represent an East Asian person (similar to blackface), continues to be used in film and theater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites multiple examples (e.g., Cloud Atlas, Grindhouse trailer parody, Balls of Fury) and historical practices (Lon Chaney's prosthetics) as anti-patterns. Evaluation: heavily caricatured makeup or prosthetics that deliberately distort features to mimic Asians should be considered offensive and unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid whitewashing — cast ethnically appropriate actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Hiring non-Asian (often white) actors to portray Asian characters — 'whitewashing' — has been a prominent historical and contemporary problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Ghost in the Shell (Scarlett Johansson), Aloha (Emma Stone), Kung Fu (David Carradine), and numerous historical film productions. The article documents harms (e.g., Anna May Wong passed over for lead roles). Evaluation: prefer casting actors who share the character's ethnicity; whitecasting major Asian roles is a clear negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayals should be realistic and avoid ethnocentric perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals of East Asians have frequently reflected an ethnocentric perception rather than realistic and authentic depictions of East Asian cultures, colors, customs, and behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether representation presents rounded, culturally-informed characters or flattens culture into exotic or othering traits. Anti-patterns include using 'Far Eastern exoticism' as a veneer to soften satire or portray difference rather than truth (e.g., The Mikado's original intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotypical tropes and caricatured character types
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes such as the 'dragon lady', 'Yellow Peril', emasculated Asian men, or socially awkward/sexually inept caricatures (e.g., Long Duk Dong) perpetuate harmful tropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists many stereotype examples (Dragon Lady, long Duk Dong, Fu Manchu). Evaluation should flag roles or narratives that rely on such tropes rather than complex characterization; consider both plot function and repeated pattern across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use exaggerated physical features or offensive prosthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical alteration (e.g., built-up cheekbones, inserted props in nostrils, fishskin eyelid casts, skin-darkening creams) used to create an 'Asian' appearance is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include Lon Chaney Sr., Jonathan Pryce in Miss Saigon (heavy eyelids/skin-darkening). Such techniques are anti-patterns; they transform actors into caricatures rather than enabling authentic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor intra-Asian diversity and avoid treating 'Asian' as monolith
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that films like Crazy Rich Asians were 'not Asian enough' or too narrowly Chinese highlights the need to represent ethnic, linguistic, and socio-economic diversity within Asian communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should consider whether a work erases internal diversity (ethnic groups, class, language/dialect differences, colorism). Anti-patterns include substituting one Asian ethnicity for another without justification or failing to depict local linguistic/register authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and dialect authenticity matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying characters speaking non-local or inauthentic registers (e.g., replacing Singaporean English with British/American English) can be grounds for criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites Crazy Rich Asians for language choices. Evaluate whether language use undermines regional specificity or flattens cultural identity for audience convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage communities and advisors; reimagine problematic works collaboratively
rubrics_metrics.description: When works or productions provoke complaints (e.g., The Mikado), engaging advisory groups and redesigning concepts can resolve issues and produce more acceptable productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York Gilbert & Sullivan Players redesigned The Mikado with East Asian-American theatre professionals; Lamplighters reset The Mikado to Renaissance-era Milan. Positive practice: consult affected communities and adapt staging/casting to remove offensive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive in animation and voice casting
rubrics_metrics.description: Animated portrayals (e.g., Siamese cats in Lady and the Tramp, Bugs Bunny Nips the Nips) and voice acting choices can propagate racist stereotypes and accent caricatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include character design, exaggerated physical/behavioral traits, and voice/accents. Anti-patterns: exaggerated 'slanted eyes', buckteeth, mocking accents, or using stereotyped behaviors to signal ethnicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fetishization, model-minority framing, and emasculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals that fetishize Asian bodies/identities, promote 'model minority' myths, or emasculate Asian men (e.g., erasure of Asian male romantic leads) are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents contests over lead roles and critiques of emasculation in adaptations (e.g., To All the Boys... male love interests changed). Evaluate whether narrative choices reduce people to fantasies or social myths rather than full subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize historical and institutional constraints shaping casting
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical rules and industry practices (e.g., the Hays Code's anti-miscegenation rules, studio 'illusion' priorities) influenced casting decisions and whitewashing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of contemporary works should be informed by history; where historical constraints existed, documentation and critique of those causes is relevant. This is less an actionable production guideline than contextual criterion for critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call out and avoid reusing racist source material without adaptation or critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Works adapted from racist or exoticizing source material (e.g., Madame Butterfly, certain melodramas) need careful handling to avoid perpetuating harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptations should interrogate original material's biases; uncritical remakes risk repeating racist portrayals. Reviewers should judge whether adaptation updates, critiques, or simply reproduces problematic elements.
